title: Zero Trust
summary: Zero trust is a security model that removes implicit trust from network location and instead evaluates every request against identity, device posture, context and policy before granting the least access needed. The traditional perimeter assumed that anything inside the corporate network was trustworthy and anything outside was not, and remote work, cloud services and mobile devices destroyed that assumption. Zero trust replaces it with explicit verification, so a request from a corporate subnet receives no more privilege than the same request from a home network. Core components include a strong identity provider with phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, a policy decision point that consumes signals from device management and threat detection, segmentation that constrains lateral movement, and pervasive logging so that every decision can be audited after the fact. Reference architectures describe the model in terms of a policy engine, a policy administrator and policy enforcement points, which gives architects shared vocabulary when planning a migration. Migration is incremental, because few organisations can rebuild identity, endpoint management and network policy at the same time. A realistic sequence strengthens identity first, then device assurance, then application-level access brokers that replace broad network reachability, and finally workload-level policy for the highest-value systems. The hard parts are cultural and operational rather than technical: legacy applications that cannot express fine-grained authorisation, service accounts holding standing privilege, and business processes that depend on unrestricted file-share access. Zero trust also fails when telemetry is poor, because a policy engine fed stale or incomplete device data will either block legitimate work or wave through compromised endpoints. Mature implementations measure the share of access decisions made by policy, count standing privileged accounts, and test how quickly access can be revoked.
objectives: You will be able to explain why network location is not an authentication signal and what replaces it.
You will be able to describe the roles of the policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement point.
You will be able to identify standing privilege and implicit trust relationships in a real environment.
You will be able to design an incremental migration order across identity, device assurance and application access.
You will be able to evaluate whether telemetry quality is sufficient for policy decisions and where it misleads.
You will be able to measure zero trust progress with defensible metrics rather than vendor claims.

beginner.definition: Zero trust is a security approach that stops treating your own network as safe. It checks every request based on who is asking, what device they use and what they want, then grants the smallest access needed. Being inside the office network gives you no special trust. The name means there is no automatic trust based on location.
beginner.whyItMatters: The old idea was a castle with a wall: safe inside, dangerous outside. Remote work, cloud services and personal phones broke that idea. Attackers who get one password now find themselves already inside the walls. Zero trust removes that free pass, so a stolen account gets only what it is allowed. It also forces you to log decisions, which helps you understand incidents afterwards.
howItWorks: Every request must prove identity, usually with multi-factor authentication, meaning two different proofs.
The system also checks the device: is it managed, patched and free of known problems?
A policy engine compares the request with your rules and decides allow, deny or limited access.
Access is granted to a specific application or data set, not to a whole network.
Every decision and session is logged, so you can review what happened later.
You start with identity and your most valuable systems, then expand step by step.
beginner.example: Think of a modern hotel. The front desk does not hand you a key to every room. Your card opens your room, the gym during opening hours and nothing else. If you lose the card, it can be cancelled within seconds. Staff have different cards, and each open is recorded. That is zero trust: identity plus context, checked every time, with the smallest access that still lets you do your job.
takeaways: Location is not proof of trust; verify every request on its own merits.
Give the smallest access that works, and grant it for a limited time.
Good telemetry matters, because bad device data leads to bad decisions.
